definition: showing rude or arrogant lack of respect
memoryTip: In-solent: so rude you feel the insult — cheeky disrespect.
correctPassage: The student gave an insolent answer that left the principal speechless.
wrongPassages: The nurse was insolent when she gently calmed the frightened child.
His insolent apology showed deep regret for what he had done.
They praised her insolent manners at the formal dinner.

definition: the process of spreading more widely
memoryTip: Diffuse = scatter: ideas or particles spreading out.
correctPassage: The diffusion of new teaching methods reached rural schools within a year.
wrongPassages: The diffusion of the crowd into one tiny room made movement impossible.
She practiced diffusion by locking every window against the wind.
The museum's diffusion of the statue kept it sealed in a vault.

definition: spoken or done without preparation
memoryTip: Ex tempore = out of the moment — no notes, no rehearsal.
correctPassage: When the slides failed, she delivered an extemporaneous talk that still won the room.
wrongPassages: His extemporaneous speech had been rehearsed for three solid weeks.
They filed an extemporaneous report after months of careful drafting.
The extemporaneous ceremony followed a script printed the day before.

definition: tending to remind one of something
memoryTip: Reminisce = remember: reminiscent things spark old memories.
correctPassage: The alley was reminiscent of the neighborhood where she grew up.
wrongPassages: The brand-new design was reminiscent of nothing anyone had ever seen.
He stayed reminiscent so he would never look back on the past.
A totally blank memory made the photo feel deeply reminiscent.

definition: deep-seated hostility or active opposition
memoryTip: Enemy + -ity: the state of being someone's enemy.
correctPassage: Decades of enmity made even a handshake between the leaders unlikely.
wrongPassages: Their lifelong enmity was the reason they never stopped helping each other.
The club's enmity toward new members showed in warm welcome dinners.
She felt only enmity for the friend who had always stood by her.

definition: abundant in quantity or supply
memoryTip: Copy lots: copious means there's plenty to go around.
correctPassage: She took copious notes during the lecture and barely looked up.
wrongPassages: The drought left only copious water in the cracked riverbed.
His copious vocabulary consisted of fewer than twenty words.
They packed a copious lunch: one cracker and a dry raisin.

definition: find a way around an obstacle or rule
memoryTip: Circum- (around) + vent (go): slip around the barrier.
correctPassage: The startup found a legal way to circumvent the outdated licensing rule.
wrongPassages: She tried to circumvent the mountain by tunneling straight through its core.
He would circumvent every problem by meeting it head-on with full force.
They circumvented the fence by climbing over the exact center of it.

definition: make free from bacteria or other living microorganisms
memoryTip: Make sterile: kill germs so nothing can grow.
correctPassage: Lab techs sterilize the petri dishes before each experiment.
wrongPassages: They sterilize the garden by planting more flowers every spring.
She sterilized the messy desk by stacking more papers on top.
He sterilized the spoiled milk by leaving it on the warm counter.

definition: regularly found among a people or in a particular place
memoryTip: En-demos: native to a people/place, not a one-time visitor.
correctPassage: Malaria remains endemic in several lowland regions of the country.
wrongPassages: The virus was endemic for a single weekend and then vanished forever.
Snow is endemic to the desert, appearing only once every few centuries.
An endemic guest visited the town once and never returned.

definition: only slightly related to the main matter; diverging
memoryTip: Off on a tangent: barely touching the main point.
correctPassage: His tangential comments about lunch delayed the budget vote.
wrongPassages: Her tangential evidence proved every claim in the central argument.
The tangential chapter was the book's main thesis from start to finish.
They called the plan tangential because it addressed the core problem directly.

definition: a stock of skills, pieces, or roles one can perform
memoryTip: Your repertory of tricks: the set of things you can do.
correctPassage: The pianist expanded her repertoire to include modern jazz standards.
wrongPassages: His repertoire for the role was a single line he still had not learned.
The empty repertoire folder held every song the band had ever played.
She expanded her repertoire by erasing every song she already knew.

definition: extend out beyond a surface or line
memoryTip: Jut out like a jaw: stick out past the edge.
correctPassage: Balconies jut over the street, shading the sidewalk below.
wrongPassages: The smooth wall seemed to jut inward, leaving no edge at all.
They jut the carpet flat so nothing stuck up from the floor.
The lake jutted deep underground with no surface shoreline.

definition: relating to earthquakes; of enormous or sudden impact
memoryTip: Seismograph quake energy: huge shakes, literal or figurative.
correctPassage: The merger sent a seismic shock through the entire industry.
wrongPassages: The seismic change was so tiny that no one noticed it at all.
They called the quiet nap a seismic event in the afternoon schedule.
A seismic whisper barely disturbed the air in the library.

definition: a difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation
memoryTip: Stuck in a pickle: a predicament is a hard spot to escape.
correctPassage: Without a spare tire, they faced a real predicament on the remote road.
wrongPassages: After years of careful saving, their predicament was a fully funded retirement.
Her predicament was so easy that she solved it in under a minute.
They celebrated the predicament of a perfectly planned vacation.

definition: responsibility for a fault or wrong; blameworthiness
memoryTip: Culpa = blame: culpability is how much fault you carry.
correctPassage: The inquiry assessed each manager's culpability for the safety failure.
wrongPassages: His clear innocence increased his culpability in the public eye.
They awarded culpability medals to the volunteers who helped most.
She felt deep culpability for a success she had fully earned.

definition: the act of distributing or spreading over a wide area
memoryTip: Disperse = scatter: dispersion is the spread itself.
correctPassage: Wide dispersion of the seeds helped the plants colonize new slopes.
wrongPassages: The dispersion of the troops into one bunker left the field empty.
Tight dispersion packed every book into a single sealed box.
Her dispersion of secrets meant she told no one anything at all.

definition: dig out earth and uncover by digging
memoryTip: Ex-cavate: dig out a cavity in the ground.
correctPassage: Crews will excavate the foundation before the concrete pour.
wrongPassages: They excavate the pile higher by dumping more dirt on top each day.
She excavated the shelf by carefully stacking more boxes on it.
Builders excavate the roof when they add another floor above.

definition: adorn with chains of flowers, lights, or fabric hung in loops
memoryTip: Festival loops: hang decorations in draping curves.
correctPassage: Volunteers festoon the hall with paper lanterns before the dance.
wrongPassages: They festoon the room by stripping every decoration from the walls.
She festooned the blank wall with a single flat sticker in the center.
Workers festoon the floor by scrubbing it until it shone.

definition: ordinary written or spoken language, as opposed to poetry
memoryTip: Not verse: prose is everyday sentences, not meter and rhyme.
correctPassage: Her prose is clear and spare, with almost no figurative flourish.
wrongPassages: The poet's prose used strict rhyme schemes on every other line.
He danced a flowing prose across the stage without saying a word.
Their prose chorus rose in perfect four-part harmony.

definition: angry or bitter conflict; struggle
memoryTip: Strive into conflict: strife is fighting and discord.
correctPassage: Political strife delayed the reconstruction for several years.
wrongPassages: Years of strife brought the neighbors closer than ever before.
The strife of the peaceful garden soothed everyone who entered.
They enjoyed the strife of a quiet evening with no disagreements.
